title: Live from MAICON 2025: Building AAA's First AI Arbitrator — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Leonard treats AI’s effects on lawyer skills and professional formation as questions for exploration using GPT-5. The supplied evidence provides no model answers, concrete training proposal, measured outcomes, or expressed view on whether automation threatens expertise reproduction, so her position on the cluster’s proposition cannot be determined.
qs: I fed those into GPT-5 to ask, "How will these skills be impacted in a world of AI disruption?
And on the flip side, how might a new lawyer use AI to accelerate their own formation?" I was happy I had just done that exercise, because I could offer it to this law student.

st.t: Selective augmentation: Verification constrains uneven productivity gains
st.an: The source constructively explores AI’s possible effects on new-lawyer skills and formation using an established competency framework, which is relevant to the cluster’s junior-development tension. However, it reports neither findings nor a clear position on selective augmentation, verification, retained lawyer judgment, or staffing consequences.

And on the flip side, how might a new lawyer use AI to accelerate their own formation?" I was happy I had just done that exercise, because I could offer it to this law student.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s framing that AI should address existing shortages in civil-justice capacity and materially develops its bounded-dispute-resolution proposition through AAA’s planned documents-only construction launch, industry consultation and closed-record design. It also supports the cluster’s caution that claimed procedural benefits remain predictions rather than measured outcomes and separately identifies deepfake authenticity as a distinct reliability risk.
qs: And this first use case is just documents-only construction cases.

Bridget McCormack: This is the problem with the civil justice system generally: there are not enough humans to help people with civil justice problems, and there are certainly not enough humans to hear every individual person in all of those cases.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source endorses practitioner-led experimentation before technological certainty and materially develops that agenda through AAA’s incremental, user-informed implementation process, alongside AI-assisted redesign of lawyer training. Its bounded deployment and attention to synthetic-evidence risks are consistent with preserving reliability and judicial legitimacy, although outcomes remain unproven.
qs: We've been building things for our users, building things for our teams, and learning along the way.
We're actually talking to users right now to see what they want, instead of us deciding what we want.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source extends the engagement-first proposition with concrete deployment practices: AAA is consulting users to shape expansion and promises transparency about system design and safeguards. It remains prospective, however, offering launch commitments and planned independent research rather than evidence of effectiveness or trustworthiness.
qs: We're actually talking to users right now to see what they want, instead of us deciding what we want.
We're really eager to show you how we've built it, what the guardrails are, why it's trustworthy.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source accepts legal AI as service and organisational redesign and adds concrete methods: competency-based redesign of lawyer development, user-led prioritisation of AI-arbitrator use cases, and planned transparency around safeguards. These are proposed approaches rather than evidence of successful outcomes.
qs: It was fantastic—really a great starting place for thinking about what new structures you might build to train lawyers.
We're actually talking to users right now to see what they want, instead of us deciding what we want.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: AAA accepts the need for selective, human-supervised deployment and concretely develops it through a bounded, AI-native arbitration model. Its case-type-by-case-type rollout, reliance on domain expertise and data, preservation of human involvement and user choice, and claim-clarification workflow provide a specific operating-model application of the cluster’s proposition, though projected efficiency and fairness gains remain prospective.
qs: But there will be other disputes where two business owners might say, "For these disputes that are governed by this contract, and there are only a few ways the dispute arises, we’d like to send all those immediately to an AI-native option."  I should have mentioned at the top: we have a human in the loop throughout the process.
The AI arbitrator that can reason—we're going to roll that out case type by case type, because we need to train it on our own expertise and data.

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s distinction between bounded AI assistance and autonomous adjudication. AAA’s planned deployment retains a human arbitrator, preserves party choice, starts with a narrow documents-only use case, and expands case by case where suitable expertise and data exist. Its efficiency and confidence claims are predictions rather than measured results, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caution.

kp.k: AI translates partner edits into junior-lawyer writing instruction
kp.d: McCormack recounts an appellate practice partner's experience using Claude to compare associate drafts with her revisions and explain the lessons to junior lawyers. The reported benefit is making tacit writing expertise teachable, rather than merely producing corrected work. This is a secondhand mentoring anecdote, not a measured training outcome.
qs: Did you try feeding their draft and your draft to Claude and just asking Claude to think about what your changes did to the writing, and then how to take those lessons and translate them for lawyers who are still learning how to take their writing up a notch?
I could just take their work and get it to where I needed it to be, but that's not helpful for them the next time around.

kp.k: AI can help redesign professional development around existing competencies
kp.d: Leonard describes feeding IAALS's Foundations for Practice competencies into GPT-5 to explore AI's effects on skills and opportunities to accelerate lawyer formation. She reports that the underlying survey covered 24,000 lawyers, recalls 76 skills and five core competencies, and places the report about 11 years earlier. She recommends the exercise for professional development teams and talent officers; McCormack frames the report as a starting point for new training structures. The claimed usefulness reflects Leonard's experience, not a validation of GPT-5's recommendations.
qs: Foundations for Practice, which surveyed 24,000 lawyers and asked them what attributes of new lawyers set them apart as exceptional attorneys.
I think it identified 76 different skills, which is a little overwhelming. But there are five core competencies that range from practitioner to communicator.
How will these skills be impacted in a world of AI disruption? And on the flip side, how might a new lawyer use AI to accelerate their own formation?

kp.k: AAA plans narrowly scoped, multi-agent AI arbitration
kp.d: McCormack says AAA announced in September a November 3rd launch of its first AI arbitrator, initially restricted to documents-only construction cases. She describes an AI-native case management system developed over about nine or ten months, with approximately 80 agents operating across a case's lifecycle. Significant cost and resolution-time reductions are her forecasts, not demonstrated results in the transcript.
qs: We announced in September that on November 3rd, we are going live with the first AI arbitrator.
And this first use case is just documents-only construction cases. We started with a pretty discrete case type, and it's a multi-agent architecture.
I think my team says they're up to 80 agents that operate across the life of an arbitration case that goes to the AI arbitrator.
It's going to significantly reduce cost and time to resolution, and we're pretty excited for the world to see it.

kp.k: AI arbitration retains humans and requires bilateral consent
kp.d: McCormack describes parties participating in the filing process and a trained human arbitrator remaining involved throughout. Both parties must choose the AI option; future contractual adoption is anticipated rather than established. Removing the human arbitrator is only a possible future consideration. She expects continued demand for human-led processes, including disputes where maintaining an ongoing relationship matters.
qs: I should have mentioned at the top: we have a human in the loop throughout the process.
We have a panel of arbitrators trained to work on this process.
At some point, if there are users who want us to unplug the human, we can definitely think about what that looks like.
Both sides have to agree. It's all optional.
And so they just want more human involvement along the way, because it's as much a relationship-saving process as it is a dispute resolution process.

kp.k: Existing expertise and bounded records determine initial deployment
kp.d: McCormack explains that AAA selected construction disputes because it possesses extensive documents-only awards, expertise and industry relationships, and because resolving ongoing-project disputes efficiently matters to users. Awards informed a handbook used to train agents. Excluding testimony and testimony transcripts simplifies the initial task. She likens the bounded record to Adam Unikowsky's proposed use of AI for appellate oral argument, presenting that comparison as an analogy rather than deployment evidence.
qs: We have all this expertise and all these awards that we were able to turn into the handbook to train the agents that are working across the arbitration process.
It's also the case that it's fairly simple: the AI arbitrator doesn't have to listen to testimony or even review transcripts of testimony.
And it's a contained, closed data set. So this is sort of like that—a similar idea.

kp.k: AAA combines operational adoption with iterative user testing
kp.d: McCormack situates the arbitrator within several years of AI point solutions and case management integration, including tools for parties and arbitrators and arbitrator training. She says AAA learned which work to perform internally or with partners. Development recruited lawyers, arbitrators, law students and professors to identify usability problems during sprints, with continued iteration expected after launch. An independent academic white paper and explanations of guardrails are promised, but their findings are not supplied.
qs: We had to figure out what we could do well ourselves, what we did better with a partner, and what we should just let a partner do altogether.
we already have AI support built into our legacy case management system for parties and for arbitrators, and we've been training arbitrators on how to use those tools.
We wanted them to use it as first-time users who know nothing about arbitration: How does it work for you? Where did you find it confusing?
We'll release a white paper with it by an independent academic researcher.

kp.k: Party confirmation is intended to strengthen procedural fairness
kp.d: McCormack describes agents restating each party's claims, elements, evidence and legal support, allowing confirmation or correction before an explained award. She predicts this will increase confidence by making parties feel understood. She invokes procedural justice literature supporting acceptance of adverse outcomes when people feel heard, but gives no study details or results demonstrating that this particular system achieves those benefits.
qs: Look, I think these are your claims. I think these are the elements of your claims. This is the evidence you have that supports those claims. And this is the law that you believe says you should win on those claims. Did I get that right?
Maybe there was another claim that wasn't perfectly pled, but this process gives them an opportunity to make sure they were heard.
You can give them a bad result, and if they feel heard and understood, they will still grow more confident in the process.
I think it's a game changer that this will actually grow parties' confidence in the process, because they'll be able to see that it understood what they were complaining about.

kp.k: Civil justice capacity limits motivate a broader AI rationale
kp.d: McCormack argues that civil justice systems lack enough people both to help those with legal problems and to hear every litigant fully. Leonard frames appropriately situated AI as potentially responding to the human need to be heard rather than simply removing humanity. This is a broader access-to-justice argument, distinct from the initial business-to-business construction offering and its anticipated efficiency gains.
qs: The way people think about it now is that you're removing the humanity from the system. But in a lot of ways, you're actually responding to the human need to be heard—because there aren't enough humans to hear all the other humans.

This is the problem with the civil justice system generally: there are not enough humans to help people with civil justice problems, and there are certainly not enough humans to hear every individual person in all of those cases.

kp.k: Expansion separates universal case management from specialized adjudication
kp.d: McCormack plans replacement of AAA's entire case management system by the end of 2027, supporting all case types and user-selected degrees of AI involvement. Reasoning arbitrators would expand case type by case type, conditional on relevant expertise and data, using general front-end agents plus specialized agents. Payer-provider healthcare and no-fault caseloads are possible next areas; her CTO expects several additions in 2026. These are plans and expectations, not completed deployments.
qs: We will replace our entire case management system by the end of 2027 with an AI-native platform
The AI arbitrator that can reason—we're going to roll that out case type by case type, because we need to train it on our own expertise and data.
Then, for a specific dispute type, you need an additional set of agents trained on data relevant to that type of dispute.
There's a lot in the payer provider healthcare disputes—you see those in some no-fault caseloads as well.
She thinks we can get a number of new ones built in 2026.

kp.k: In-house teams express selective demand for automated dispute resolution
kp.d: McCormack reports interest from in-house teams in other industries, especially for supplier and dealer disputes. These prospective buyers identify particular caseloads rather than seeking automation of every dispute, while retaining established processes for others. The transcript reports expressions of interest and market consultation, not adoption volumes or purchasing commitments.
qs: I'm hearing from lots of—in-house teams especially, in other industries—who already have identified a case and they're like, "Oh gosh, could you do this one next? It's perfect for supplier disputes," or "It's perfect for dealer disputes."
Again, they don't want to use it for everything. They definitely want to be able to continue to use the process they used last year for certain cases.
We're actually talking to users right now to see what they want, instead of us deciding what we want.

kp.k: Generative video raises distinct training and output-related legal risks
kp.d: Leonard reports that Sora 2's invitation rollout allowed uses of copyrighted characters and likenesses under an opt-out approach, prompting backlash and a permission-first reversal for copyrighted characters. She says no lawsuits had yet arisen in that rollout discussion. McCormack separates existing training-data copyright disputes from risks created by user-generated outputs and predicts further legal action. Both question whether predictable misuse was adequately anticipated; these are their reported account and judgments, not judicial findings.
qs: They shifted back to an opt-in, permission-first model for copyrighted characters. So now rights holders are able to specify how or whether their IP can be used.
So there are no lawsuits yet, but it crystallized several tensions.
One is the issue OpenAI has been answering in text contexts, which is: How did they train this model, and was copyrighted material used to train it?
I don't know if they think it's solved by switching from opt-out to opt-in, but I bet we'll see more legal action around that in the coming weeks and months.

kp.k: Realistic synthetic video threatens confidence in evidentiary authenticity
kp.d: McCormack reports Ethan Mollick's warning that people are unprepared for indistinguishable AI video, that watermarks are easily removed, and that unwatermarked open-weight models are forthcoming. She anticipates implications for courts and lawyers and reports receiving more judicial questions about deepfakes than other topics, while qualifying that relatively few cases involve video evidence. The discussion offers a risk forecast and practitioner observation, not measured prevalence or an authentication solution.
qs: Despite years of warning, I don't think people are prepared for a world where AI videos are going to exist and no one is going to know when they are AI videos.
What Ethan said was, they do watermark videos that are created, but it's really easy to remove them.
And before long we're going to have open-weight models that aren't watermarked.
I get more questions from judges about deepfakes than anything else, even though not that many cases have video evidence.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McCormack predicts faster, cheaper and potentially more confidence-building dispute resolution through AAA's human-supervised AI arbitrator, followed by broader AI-native case management and case-specific expansion. The speakers also describe AI-assisted lawyer development and emerging legal problems from synthetic video.
pts.d:
1. AAA AI arbitrator: Bridget McCormack, speaking as AAA president, announces what she calls the first AI arbitrator, initially for documents-only construction disputes. She describes an AI-native case management system with approximately 80 agents operating across an arbitration's lifecycle and predicts significant reductions in cost and time to resolution. This is not described as fully autonomous adjudication: parties participate in checking the system's understanding, and a trained human arbitrator remains involved.
2. Procedural fairness: McCormack argues that agents can restate parties' claims, elements, evidence and legal support and invite corrections before an award explains the outcome. She predicts that this opportunity to feel heard and understood will increase confidence in the process, including among losing parties. She contrasts this with busy courts' limited capacity to engage individually with every claim. This is a predicted benefit, not a reported result from completed AI arbitrations.
3. Service differentiation: McCormack expects AI-native arbitration to become an additional, voluntarily selected dispute-resolution option, rather than replace human-led arbitration universally. Parties may prefer greater human involvement in relationship-sensitive or high-stakes matters while selecting AI-native processing for recurring, bounded commercial disputes. She also states that arbitrators will need to bring AI-enabled efficiencies to parties even in more human-led processes.
4. Expansion: McCormack commits to replacing AAA's entire case management system with an AI-native platform supporting all case types, with users choosing the degree of AI-native case management. She distinguishes this platform from the reasoning AI arbitrator, which will expand case type by case type. She reports interest from in-house teams in supplier and dealer disputes and identifies healthcare payer-provider or no-fault-related documents-only disputes as possible next applications, not confirmed launches.
5. Lawyer development: McCormack reports an unnamed appellate partner's experience using Claude to translate differences between associate drafts and partner revisions into teachable writing lessons. The reported success belongs to that partner's experience, not to a measured outcome or McCormack's own trial. Leonard separately describes her own use of GPT-5 to explore how AI might affect foundational lawyer competencies and support professional formation. McCormack endorses this as a starting point for redesigning junior-lawyer training; Leonard suggests its use by professional development and talent teams.
6. Synthetic video: Leonard describes Sora 2's rollout as exposing IP, likeness and public-trust problems, including a reported reversal from opt-out to permission-first treatment for copyrighted characters. McCormack distinguishes disputes over model training material from downstream generated content and predicts further legal action over the latter. She also anticipates difficulties for lawyers and courts when realistic AI video is hard to distinguish from authentic recordings. Her account of watermark removal and future unwatermarked open-weight models is explicitly attributed to Ethan Mollick rather than presented as her own technical finding.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal basis is McCormack's firsthand account of AAA's development work, institutional expertise, usability testing and user conversations; projected benefits are not supported here by quantified performance or outcome results.
pts.d:
For the AI arbitrator, McCormack cites roughly nine or ten months of development, preceding years of AI support-tool integration, AAA's century of arbitration experience, a substantial collection of documents-only construction awards, and relationships with construction-industry users. She says expertise and awards were turned into a handbook for training agents. Lawyers, arbitrators, law students and law professors tested the system during development sprints; the described testing focused on understanding the process, finding confusing aspects and improving usability. Arbitrators also helped build it. No sample sizes, adjudication-accuracy measurements, comparative benchmarks, cost figures or resolution-time results are supplied. An independent academic researcher's white paper is promised for release with the product, but its findings are not given.
For procedural confidence, McCormack invokes academic literature on procedural fairness and justice, particularly the relationship between feeling heard and accepting an adverse result. She does not identify specific studies or report AI-arbitrator-specific validation. Her comparison with courts also draws on judicial experience reviewing decisions and hearing parties complain that issues had not been addressed.
For demand and expansion, the evidence is reported conversations with construction users and in-house teams, existing industry relationships and early market consultation—not adoption statistics. McCormack attributes the expectation of progressively faster development and several new case types in 2026 to CTO Diana Didia.
For lawyer development, the Claude example is a secondhand, single-user success anecdote. Leonard's GPT-5 account is a firsthand exploratory exercise. Leonard describes the IAALS Foundations for Practice report as based on a survey of 24,000 lawyers and identifying approximately 76 skills and five core competencies; that survey supplies a framework for her exercise, not evidence that AI improves training outcomes. Her statement that reviewing the skills manually would take months is an informal estimate.
For synthetic video, the speakers rely on rollout events, reported rights-holder objections, examples of generated videos, McCormack's observations and questions received from judges, and external commentary. Their forecasts of further litigation and evidentiary complications are not supported by quantified incidence or court-outcome data in the transcript.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The announced initial launch is November 3, 2025; broader case-type development is anticipated in 2026 and platform replacement by the end of 2027, subject to consent, human involvement, suitable data and user demand.
pts.d:
At the time of this 2025 episode, the AI arbitrator is a forthcoming offering announced in September, not a service for which the speakers report completed live cases. McCormack gives November 3 as its go-live date. Initial scope is documents-only B2B construction disputes: the arbitrator need not hear testimony or review testimony transcripts, and the case materials form a bounded dataset. Both parties must opt in when filing; McCormack anticipates future contractual selection, but says no contracts currently specify the new process.
The launch retains human involvement throughout, including a trained human arbitrator. Removing that arbitrator is only a possible future consideration if users request it, with no commitment or timetable. Human-led processes will remain available. McCormack expects ongoing iteration from user feedback during an unspecified initial period of months and proposes reporting uptake after a few months.
The end-of-2027 commitment concerns AAA's case management platform across all case types, not an AI adjudicator capable of handling every dispute. AI arbitrator expansion depends on having the expertise and dispute-specific data to train additional agents. The next documents-only category is under investigation and subject to market consultation. Several additions in 2026 are a development expectation attributed to the CTO, not a guaranteed schedule.
The lawyer-development examples describe present experimentation rather than a dated profession-wide forecast. The video segment situates Sora 2's invite-only release roughly two weeks earlier. Leonard says no lawsuits have yet arisen in the rollout discussion, while McCormack separately references existing training-data litigation and predicts additional generated-content legal action in the coming weeks and months. The broader forecast of unreliable video evidence has no precise date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate target is commercial construction arbitration; prospective effects extend to corporate legal buyers, arbitrators, junior-lawyer training, courts and people affected by synthetic media.
pts.d:
Construction businesses and their lawyers are the initial users, with predicted savings and faster resolution intended to keep ongoing projects moving. Parties also receive opportunities to correct the agents' understanding of their submissions and obtain explanations of outcomes. AAA's teams and arbitrators work within an AI-native workflow, while trained human arbitrators remain involved rather than being described as displaced.
Corporate in-house teams are prospective buyers of additional dispute-resolution options, particularly for recurring supplier and dealer caseloads. Healthcare payer-provider and some no-fault caseloads are potential later markets. Parties with continuing commercial relationships may retain greater human involvement. The choice concerns a differentiated service offering rather than compulsory AI use.
Junior associates, law students and other developing lawyers may receive more explicit writing feedback and AI-assisted development plans. Partners, judges, legal educators, professional development teams and talent officers are identified as potential users of these training approaches. The transcript does not predict specific staffing reductions or changes to law-firm leverage.
McCormack situates procedural responsiveness against wider civil-justice capacity shortages affecting people whose problems cannot receive sufficient human attention. However, the announced product serves B2B construction disputes; the transcript does not demonstrate that it closes the access-to-justice gap for individuals unable to obtain legal help. That broader problem supplies context for the proposed confidence and participation benefits.
Judges, lawyers and courts face possible difficulties assessing video authenticity. Copyright holders, creators, studios, talent agencies, unions, people whose likenesses are used and the wider public face the legal and trust consequences described in the Sora 2 discussion.
